title: A review flow that keeps its place
summary: A synthetic frontend case study about readable decisions, keyboard access, and preserving context during review.
highlights: Draft state kept separate from submitted state
problem: In this fictional review tool, long forms hide the information needed for the next decision. Reviewers need to inspect detail without losing the current item.
The example considers navigation, focus, and unsaved edits as parts of one workflow.
constraints: Core decisions must remain possible without a mouse.
Expanding supporting detail must not erase edits or move focus unexpectedly.
contribution: This synthetic example does not represent personal work. An engineer in this scenario would define the interaction states and build reusable, accessible review sections.
User research and production usability results are not claimed.

decisions.title: Separate the decision from its supporting detail
decisions.choice: Keep the item summary and decision controls visible, with supporting notes in labeled disclosure sections.
decisions.alternative: Show all fields and notes at once.
decisions.tradeoff: Collapsed detail reduces scanning effort, but labels must be specific enough for readers to know what they will reveal.

decisions.title: Make unsaved work a first-class state
decisions.choice: Model draft edits separately from the saved response and ask before discarding meaningful changes.
decisions.alternative: Reset local form state whenever the selected item changes.
decisions.tradeoff: Draft state adds transitions and tests. It avoids accidental data loss when navigation and editing overlap.

results.claim: The design demonstrates a summary-first review flow with explicit draft and saved states.
results.basis: Synthetic design discussion only. No user study, accessibility certification, or measured productivity gain is claimed.

limitations: Accessible primitives do not establish that a complete application is accessible. Real assistive-technology testing remains necessary.
lessons: Focus behavior and data persistence should be designed together, not added after the happy path.
nextSteps: For a real project, test rapid navigation, partially completed forms, failed saves, and keyboard-only review.
